comment.value:
The paper introduces Time-Embedded Algorithm Unrolling (TE-Unroll) for deep learning–based MRI reconstruction, inspired by connections between vector AMP and diffusion models. The proposed method incorporates time-conditioned proximal networks (via FiLM embeddings), learnable time-varying scalars for data-fidelity weighting, and Onsager correction. It applies to multiple unrolling schemes (e.g., VSQP, ADMM) with ResNet or U-Net proximals. Extensive experiments on fastMRI knee and brain datasets at acceleration factors of 4/6/8 show consistent PSNR/SSIM improvements over shared and unshared baselines, with little parameter overhead. Ablation studies on unroll depth, optimizers, and qualitative results further validate the approach.

In the initial review, multiple concerns were raised by the reviewers, including questioning the utility and significance of the (improved) images reconstructed, the absence of comparison with the state-of-the-art baseline models, the lack of clarity around the notion of efficiency of the proposed method, and the poor motivation of the work. However, during the rebuttal period, the authors were able to sufficiently and convincingly address most of the reviewers' concerns, prompting the reviewers to update their scores. 

Keeping in mind the rebuttal posed by the authors and the subsequent changes promised in the final manuscript, this is a well-motivated, technically solid work backed up by extensive experiments and ablation studies on open-source datasets. Other strengths of the paper are: 
- Novel model that borrows the advantages from the time-embedding design in the diffusion model and the vector AMP algorithm
- Well-organized paper and easy to read
- Extensive experiments on the NYU fastMRI dataset are adequate, and evaluation is performed on different unrolling baselines
- The anecdotal human evaluation results gathered during the rebuttal period further strengthen the story

author_final_remarks.value:
We would like to sincerely thank the Reviewers, Area Chairs, and Senior Area Chairs for the time, expertise, and constructive feedback devoted to our submission. We are encouraged by the reviewers’ positive recognition of our work, commending the novelty of our time (iteration)-dependent unrolling framework (**All Reviewers**), while highlighting the generality of our framework to other iterative algorithms (**Reviewer Ea5r**), the comprehensiveness of our experiments  (**Reviewers Ed3h and Bi9Y**) and how we “recast unrolling methods through an information-theoretic and free-energy perspective” (**Reviewer Ea5r**).

**During the rebuttal,** we provided substantial additional experiments and analyses to address the concerns raised by the reviewers, focusing mainly on:

- Ablation studies (experiments on different model sizes, time-embedding hyperparameters, and validation on non-uniform sampling masks)
- Comparisons to diffusion-based models for an even more comprehensive assessment 
- **Radiologist readings and pathology inspections** to highlight the subtle and diagnostically important improvements of our method, beyond simple quantitative metrics

Consequently, three of the four reviewers indicated that their concerns were addressed, with resulting assessments reflecting a **favorable stance toward acceptance (Reviewers D5F5, Ed3h, and Ea5r). Reviewer D5F5** also stated they would increase their score following the discussion. 

**Although we were unable to engage directly with Reviewer Bi9Y, we addressed their comments comprehensively in the rebuttal** and believe the provided clarifications resolve the raised points.

In the revised manuscript, we will include the additional experiments as well as minor revisions conducted during the rebuttal period.

We appreciate the constructive engagement from all involved in this process and hope the final decision will take into account the positive developments and strengthened evidence resulting from the discussion phase.
\
\
Warm regards,
\
Authors of submission 26829

rebuttal.value:
We sincerely thank you for your thoughtful feedback. We are pleased to hear that the idea of employing a time-dependent proximal operator was seen as meaningful, and that the comprehensiveness of our experiments was appreciated. We are also grateful for the opportunity to address your concerns and further elaborate on our contributions.
\
\
**(W1) Degree of improvement achieved by our method.**  

Thank you for raising this important comment. Indeed the quantitative metrics reported in the tables do not necessarily do justice to the subtle improvements afforded by our method. Thus, to show the strength of our method beyond quantitative metrics reported in the text, we worked with a radiologist who provided their expert opinion. While there was not enough time for a full reader study during the rebuttal period, a radiologist (30+ years of experience), *blindly reviewed* the reconstructions included in our paper. The radiologist's comments are included below:

- Figure 3 (Middle) exhibits aliasing artifacts in the distal femoral metaphysis medially on PD-weighted images for VSQP, Unshared-VSQP, ADMM, Unshared-ADMM. The artifacts are effectively removed in the proposed method (ours).

- Figure 3 (Bottom) shows blurring in the right occipital lobe in VSQP, Unshared-VSQP, ADMM, Unshared-ADMM. This is notably improved in the proposed method, where the gyri and sulci appear sharper.

- Figure 4 (Top) shows visible aliasing artifacts in the central aspect of the distal femoral condyle of the inset for VSQP, Unshared-VSQP, ADMM, and Unshared-ADMM. This artifact is removed in the proposed method. The prominent penetrating intraosseous vessel at the lateral aspect of the proximal tibia (lower left on the image) appears sharper in proposed method, though overall image sharpness is similar among methods.

- Figure 4 (Middle): There is an oblong, hypointense appearing  aliasing artifact on the non-fat saturated PD-weighted images of the knee joint, just distal to the posteromedial femoral condyle, seen on VSQP, Unshared-VSQP, ADMM, and Unshared-ADMM, when compared to the reference. This artifact is removed from the image for the proposed method. Thus, only the proposed method accurately resembles the reference image. 

- Figure 4 (Bottom) reveals aliasing artifacts in VSQP, Unshared-VSQP, ADMM, Unshared-ADMM, depicted as curvilinear, oblique hypointense signal in the occipital lobe. The artifact is nearly completely removed in Unshared-ADMM, and only vaguely seen. The artifact is completely removed in ours, most accurately resembling the reference image.

Additionally, we also reconstructed several **annotated pathology cases from the FastMRI+ dataset** (DOI:10.1038/s41597-022-01255-z), and the radiologist also reviewed these. Note that these were not included in the original submission. The radiologist noted the following:  

- On the reference image there is a focal area of T2-hyperintense signal, most consistent with a partial/full thickness cartilage defect in the anteromedial trochlea. Images reconstructed by VSQP, Unshared-VSQP, ADMM, and Unshared-ADMM reveal significant blurring in this area. Proposed method shows the least amount of blurring compared to other methods, and shows the hyperintense region in the trochlear articular cartilage with the most fidelity compared to the reference data.

Unfortunately, we cannot include new figures here, due to NeurIPS's rebuttal policy, but representative examples and quotes will be included in our final manuscript. We will also add arrows to the figures to emphasize the differences highlighted by the radiologist. 

We would like to emphasize that while our quantitative improvements in Table 1 may appear modest, we believe that **these radiologist readings really highlight the improvements made by our method** that are critical for diagnostic purposes. We thank you again for this suggestion that will substantially strengthen our work.
\
\
**(W2) Core technical contribution of the paper.**  
We appreciate the opportunity to clarify this point. Indeed, AMP and its variants have been explored in the context of algorithm unrolling, as described in the text. One line of work ([11, 12] in the original submission) reparameterizes the encoding matrix ${\bf E}$ and ${\bf E}^H$, which affects the Onsager correction term. Another approach [33, 42] keeps the encoding matrix fixed, but trains distinct (unshared) proximal operators using neural networks at each iteration. These distinct proximal operators operate *without awareness of temporal (or equivalently iteration) information* (i.e., unshared in our terminology). Finally, some methods [33, 66] combine the above two strategies by jointly training both the system matrix and the proximal operators. 

Our method is technically distinct from these approaches in several key ways:

1) We keep the system matrix ${\bf E}$ fixed, since this is known from MR physics, and use a single shared proximal operator modeled by a neural network, but introduce iteration-awareness via a time-embedding technique, enabling the network to behave differently at each unrolling stage. This is distinct from the unshared proximal operators used in AMP-type algorithm unrolling approaches discussed earlier.

2) Our method is inspired by the structure of VAMP, rather than AMP. To the best of our knowledge, our work represents the first attempt to integrate VAMP with algorithm unrolling to solve computational imaging inverse problems.

3) We propose time-embedded ResNet and U-Net-based proximal operators for inverse problems in MRI. In particular, for the ResNet-based proximal operator that has been used in several MRI reconstruction works, we introduce a novel time-embedding module with a scaling factor, as described in Equation (16). For the U-Net-based proximal operator, we adapt the U-Net architecture from diffusion models, making several adjustments to reduce model size to make it suitable for inverse problems in MRI.

We appreciate your encouraging feedback. We are glad you found the extension of FiLM-based networks for iteration-dependent residual corrections to be novel, and our new interpretation of unrolling based on VAMP insightful. We are also encouraged that you found our framework to be general and the experimental results impressive.
\
\
**(W1) Formal proof of second-moment matching or energy invariance missing.**  
We agree that a formal proof of second-moment matching is desirable. Second-moment matching is typically evaluated by examining the estimated variances $ \upsilon_x^{t}$ and $ \upsilon_z^{t} $ across iterations, as in Eq. (9) \& (11). However, even if consistent trends are empirically observed in these estimates, this would not constitute a formal proof. This is further complicated in our case, as we hypothesize that a time-embedded neural network models all update steps in Eq. (10)-(11), and the learnable scalar parameter $\rho^t$ encapsulates the entire process described in Eq. (9). As a result, $\upsilon_x^{t}$ and $\upsilon_z^{t}$ are embedded within black-box neural modules and are not explicitly accessible.

Instead, to indirectly assess whether second-moment matching holds, we analyzed the relationships between intermediate estimates. Specifically, we examined the empirical differences between $\mathbf{x}^t$ and $\mathbf{u}^t$, and between $\mathbf{u}^t $ and $\mathbf{r}^{t}$ in Algorithm 1, as these pairs are intrinsically related to $\upsilon_x^{t}$ and $\upsilon_z^{t}$, respectively. If these differences remained consistently small across iterations, it provided evidence that the underlying variance estimates are stable. The empirical difference between $\mathbf{x}^t$ and the reconstructed $\mathbf{u}^t$ was reported in Appendix C. As shown in Table 5, the difference (normalized MSE) ranges from $1.01 \times 10^{-9}$ to $3.35 \times 10^{-2}$, demonstrating stable behavior. These findings suggest that second-moment matching is empirically preserved, despite the use of learned components. We will clarify these points in more detail in the final version, and clearly state the lack of a formal proof.
\
\
**(W2) Lipschitz constant or gradient explosion/vanishing of time-embedding (FiLM) layers.**  

Consider a network where at each time step $t \in$ {$1, \ldots, T$}, there are $K$ consecutive layers within the proximal operator networks composed of intermediate transformations followed by FiLM modulation. For each layer $k \in$ {$1, \ldots, K$},  

$x^{(t,k)} = \mathrm{FiLM}( f_{k}(x^{(t,k-1)}), t ),$

where $f_{k}(\cdot)$ denotes the intermediate layers (e.g., convolution + activation) preceding the FiLM block at layer $k$. Suppose each intermediate layer is Lipschitz continuous with constant $L_{k}$, and satisfies  

$\||f_{k}(x)\|| \leq L_{k} \||x\|| + \delta_{k},$

for some small $\delta_{k} \geq 0$, allowing for nonzero bias or offset when $f_{k}(0) \neq 0$. Similarly,  each FiLM block is Lipschitz continuous with constant $ \Gamma_{t,k} $, satisfying  

$\||\mathrm{FiLM}(z, t)\|| \leq \Gamma_{t,k} \||z\|| + B_{t,k}.$

The composite function then satisfies:  

$\||\mathrm{FiLM}(f_{k}(x), t)\|| \leq \Gamma_{t,k} L_{k} \||x\|| + (\Gamma_{t,k} \delta_{k} + B_{t,k}).$

Thus, the overall Lipschitz constant of the composite layer at layer $k$ and time $t$ is $\Gamma_{t,k} L_{k}$. As $T$ grows, if each $\Gamma_{t,k} L_{k}$ is strictly less than 1, their product decays exponentially, which may cause vanishing activations and hinder learning. If any are $\geq$ 1, the product can grow exponentially, causing exploding activations and instability. Thus, controlling cumulative constant, $\prod_{t=1}^T \prod_{k=1}^K \Gamma_{t,k} L_{k}$ is crucial for stable training.  

With this in mind, we agree with the reviewer that this still does not constitute a formal proof, since we do not characterize the Lipschitz constants of individual components analytically. However, we do believe this lends more credence to our empirical results. In particular, we followed the U-Net architecture and FiLM module commonly used in diffusion denoising tasks. In the diffusion model community, a large $T$ ($\geq$ 1,000) is typically used, which has been shown to result in stable training. In our unrolled networks, where we use a much smaller $T$ (e.g., 5–15), we expect that this does not lead to instability during training. We will include this discussion in the final version, and clearly state the empirical nature of our Lipschitz constant bounds.
\
\
**(Q1) Ablation studies on time-embedding module with different hyperparameters including learning curves.**  
We thank the reviewer for raising this important point. We conducted additional ablation studies to assess the effectiveness of key hyperparameters in the time-embedding module. Specifically, we evaluated: 1) the frequency of the sinusoidal encoding, 2) the embedding dimension, and 3) the number of hidden channels in the MLP layers. The experiments were conducted using a U-Net architecture with $T=10$, $R=6$ on Coronal PDFS dataset.

We sincerely appreciate your thoughtful feedback and reviewer’s careful reading of our paper. We are glad that you found our method both interesting, and that you valued our clear presentation, comprehensive experiments, the time-embedded unrolling network approach, and the observed performance gains.
\
\
**(W1, Q4) Key motivation is vague and "data-scarce" conditions are not clearly explained.**

We apologize for not making this clearer. In unrolled networks, the proximal operator, implemented implicitly by a neural network, can either be shared (fixed) or unshared (distinct) across iterations/unrolls or unshared. The former aligns well with classical optimization methods but may underperform, while the latter often enhances reconstruction quality albeit significantly increasing the number of trainable parameters. This raises the risk of overfitting, especially in data-limited settings, where one needs to *train on tens or hundreds of datasets instead of thousands*, which is common in many translational applications. This setting is what we mean by "data-scarce" conditions, and our key motivation is to improve performance in this setting without substantially increasing trainable parameters and the risk of overfitting.  To elaborate further on this overfitting issue in the data-scarce regime, when the proximal operator is varied across iterations, as in unshared unrolled networks, the number of trainable parameters increases proportionally with the number of unrolls. For example, as shown in Table 2, the unshared model has approximately ten times more parameters than the shared model when $T=10$. Despite this, under limited training data conditions (300 samples in our setting), the unshared model performs worse than the shared model, as illustrated in Table 1. We also observed that the training loss of the unshared network was lower than that of the shared network, but its performance did not generalize well on the test set, indicating a tendency to overfit under data-scarce conditions.

In summary, our primary motivation is to tackle this data-scarce setup and enhance the performance unrolled algorithms by incorporating a time (iteration)-aware proximal operator inspired by VAMP, while not substantially increasing the number of trainable parameters. Indeed retaining the shared proximal operator but introducing a time-embedding module leads to only a marginal increase in parameters. Our method consistently outperforms the baseline shared/ushared regularizer approach across various acceleration rates, producing artifact-free reconstructions with minimal computational overhead. We will further extend on these points in the final version.
\
\
**(Q1) Clarification needed on the meaning of "time".**  
Thank you for raising this point. In our work, "time" refers to the iteration index of the unrolled algorithm. We will add this clarification in the final manuscript.
\
\
**(Q2) Suggestion on time-embedded networks in dynamic MRI.**  
We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful suggestion regarding the potential application of time-embedded networks to dynamic MRI. While our current work focuses on static MRI reconstruction from retrospectively undersampled k-space data and interprets "time" as the iteration index in algorithm unrolling, we agree that extending this concept to capture true temporal dynamics, such as those present in dynamic MRI, would be an exciting future direction. The temporal dimension in dynamic MRI naturally can be aligned with the idea of time embedding, and we believe our framework could be adapted to handle dynamic MRI tasks as well. We will consider adding a brief discussion of this point in the final manuscript.
\
\
**(Q3) In Figure 1, E is not defined.**  
Thank you for noting this. E represents the encoding matrix, as in Section 2.1. We will ensure that E is clearly defined in the figure caption.
\
\
**(Q5) Clarify the meaning of the spade symbol in Table 1.**  
We apologize for the confusion. The spade symbol indicates a *shared regularizer*. We will include this description in the final manuscript.
\
\
**(Q6) Please explain whether the network is shared except for the time condition.**  
We embed time information into the *shared regularizer* within the unrolled network, as in Figure 1b. We will ensure that this point is clearly stated in the final manuscript.
\
\
**(Q7) Further explanation requested on why TE performs better on VSQP in Section 4.4.**  
As discussed in W1, the original VSQP unrolling uses a proximal operator that is fixed across unrolls/iterations. In contrast, in our method, a time-embedded proximal operator (Eq. 14) is used, where the "time" information corresponds to the iteration index of the unrolled algorithm. This iteration-dependent information enables the networks to learn iteration-specific denoising behavior and implicitly account for the associated Onsager corrections, as described in Section 3.1. We observe that this simple modification to VSQP (and similarly to ADMM) improves performance across datasets and acceleration rates in terms of PSNR and SSIM, while also reducing coherent artifacts.
\
\
**(Q8) Question regarding the value of $\tau$ in Equation 16.**  
Thank you for pointing out this omission. We set $\tau$ to 0.1, which we found heuristically to be optimal for ResNet. This information will be added to Appendix A.
\
\
**(L1) Questions about hyperparameters and generalizability to other datasets.**

We thank the reviewer for raising this question. In the unrolled networks considered here, there are several *trainable parameters*, including data fidelity parameters, $\mu$ in all methods, Lagrangian multiplier related weights, $\lambda$ in ADMM, or the Onsager correction weights, $\rho$ in our method. Thus, even though they appear as additional parameters in the algorithms, they are learned during training.

That being said, we agree that there are more hyperparameters in our method, since we use a time-embedding module. This time-embedding module adds more hyperparameters to the hyperparameters related to the neural networks used as proximal operators (ResNet and U-Net variants in our case). The hyperparameters associated with the time-embedding module include the frequency of the sinusoidal encoding, the embedding dimension, and the number of hidden channels in the MLP layers that process the time embedding. We use the same configuration across different datasets (Coronal PD, Coronal PD-FS, and Axial T2 brain), suggesting robustness across different data. Similarly, we apply the same hyperparameters across all datasets for the neural networks used as proximal operators, under which the networks consistently perform well. While these suggest generalizability, we will nonetheless clarify the increased number of hyperparameters and associated concerns in the final version.
\
\
**(L2) Suggestion to make the code publicly available.**  
We agree, and the code will be made public upon the acceptance of the paper.
\

**Additional evaluations of our method: Radiologist reading and pathology inspection.**  
While this was not a question raised by the reviewer, we wanted to mention an additional reader study we performed during the rebuttal to highlight the strengths of our method. The authors propose Time-Embedded Algorithm Unrolling (TE-Unroll) for DL-based inverse problems in MRI.

Building on the link between vector AMP and diffusion models, they: (i) make the proximal network explicitly time‐conditioned via FiLM-style embeddings; (ii) treat the data-fidelity weight and Onsager term as learnable, time-varying scalars; and (iii) show how the idea plugs into multiple unrolling schemes (VSQP, ADMM) with both ResNet and U-Net proximals. 

Experiments on the fastMRI knee (PD / PD-FS) and brain (T2) data at R = 4/6/8 undersampling demonstrate consistent PSNR/SSIM gains over shared and unshared baselines while adding <15 % extra parameters (e.g., 1.96 M vs 1.72 M for U-Net) . Extensive ablations (unroll depth, alternative optimisers) and qualitative slices support the claims. 

The paper is very interesting, in terms of embedding the # of step into the unrolled network, I do have some concerns regarding the evaluations, comparisons. I will elaborate later.

summary.value: In this paper, the authors proposed a time-dependent unrolling-based neural network for fast MRI reconstruction. Simulation experiment demonstrates its effectiveness. Addressing the typical inverse problem of compressed sensing MRI, this paper could trigger the interest of a wide range of audiences in computational imaging.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths:
(1) This paper borrows the advantages from the time-embedding design in diffusion model and vector AMP algorithm and successfully apply them in CS-MRI.
(2) This paper is well organized and easy to read.
(3) Experiments on NYU fastMRI dataset are adequate and evaluation is performed on different un-rolling baselines.

Weaknesses:
(1) Key motivation is vague.

questions.value:
(1) "Time" in the "time-embedded" is referred to as the diffusion and denoising step in diffusion models, whereas it is the iteration step in unrolling-based methods in CS-MRI. The authors might want to clarify this point.
(2) Following the last comment, it would be interesting to discuss the time-embedded networks in dynamic MRI.
(3) In Figure 1, E is not undefined in this figure.
(4) Authors mentioned the data-scarce condition in CS-MRI, which limits the unshared networks. Please detail such limitations.
(5) In Table 1, what does the spades denote?
(6) Please explain if the network in your method is shared except for the time condition.
(7) Could you explain more about why TE works better on VSQP in Section 4.4?
(8) In Equation 16, what is the value of \tau?

limitations.value:
(1) There are many hyperparameters in the proposed method, and I am curious if it could be well generalized to other datasets.
(2) I would encourage the code to be publicized.

summary.value: The paper introduces a Time-Embedded Algorithm Unrolling framework for MRI inverse problems, integrating diffusion-model time embeddings with AMP/VAMP’s Onsager corrections and data-fidelity weights as learnable, iteration-dependent functions. Each unrolled iteration leverages step-specific FiLM networks and residual corrections to achieve high-fidelity reconstructions.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
# Strengths:

- Extending FiLM-based networks to learn iteration-dependent residual corrections is novel.
- Recasting unrolling methods through an information-theoretic and free-energy perspective.
- The framework seems generalizes to any iterative reconstruction algorithm. The experimental results are impressive!

# Weaknesses:
- Section 3 maps the diffusion-model Markov chain to a VAMP-inspired unrolling, assuming unbiased estimators and free-energy conservation in Onsager corrections, but omits a formal proof of second-moment matching or energy invariance.

summary.value: This paper proposes to incorporate time information into the proximal operator within the algorithm unrolling scheme for accelerated MRI reconstruction, in order to address the trade-off in unrolled networks where sharing a proximal operator across iterations can cause artifacts, while using distinct networks per iteration leads to overfitting. The proposed method leads to on-par results with non-weight-sharing unrolling methods weight-sharing unrolling methods on uniformly 4x,6x,8x undersampled MRI data from fastMRI.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths:
- The idea of the time-dependent proximal operator to avoid using non-weight-sharing regularizers has some merits.
- The experiments are comprehensive

Weaknesses:
- The gains brought the proposed method seem marginal both quantitatively and qualitatively (Tab 1, Fig 3). Even the performance between the weight-sharing regularizers and the non-weight-sharing regularizers is close already (Tab 1). 
-  The core technical contribution of the paper is the time-embedding applied to the proximal operator within a VAMP-inspired framework, which seems limited: AMP has been explored in algorithm unrolling as also noted by the authors, and the time is embeded using FiLM.

questions.value: The gains of the proposed methods over weight-sharing methods are not obvious either.

title.value: Time-Embedded Algorithm Unrolling for Computational MRI

abstract.value: Algorithm unrolling methods have proven powerful for solving the regularized least squares problem in computational magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). These approaches unfold an iterative algorithm with a fixed number of iterations, typically alternating between a neural network-based proximal operator for regularization, a data fidelity operation and auxiliary updates with learnable parameters. While the connection to optimization methods dictate that the proximal operator network should be shared across unrolls, this can introduce artifacts or blurring. Heuristically, practitioners have shown that using distinct networks may be beneficial, but this significantly increases the number of learnable parameters, making it challenging to prevent overfitting. To address these shortcomings, by taking inspirations from proximal operators with varying thresholds in approximate message passing (AMP) and the success of time-embedding in diffusion models, we propose a time-embedded algorithm unrolling scheme for inverse problems. Specifically, we introduce a novel perspective on the iteration-dependent proximal operation in vector AMP (VAMP) and the subsequent Onsager correction in the context of algorithm unrolling, framing them as a time-embedded neural network. Similarly, the scalar weights in the data fidelity operation and its associated Onsager correction are cast as time-dependent learnable parameters. Our extensive experiments on the fastMRI dataset, spanning various acceleration rates and datasets, demonstrate that our method effectively reduces aliasing artifacts and mitigates noise amplification, achieving state-of-the-art performance. Furthermore, we show that our time-embedding strategy extends to existing algorithm unrolling approaches, enhancing reconstruction quality without increasing the computational complexity significantly. Code available at https://github.com/JN-Yun/TE-Unrolling-MRI.
